## TrailFold Daypack — Static Meta Production Brief

**Production objective:** Create three distinct 4:5 static ads for cold and warm Meta audiences. Keep the product, landing page, offer, CTA, and format consistent so the primary test variable is the **angle**. Do not add a discount or make unverified waterproof, 15-inch laptop, sustainability, durability, testimonial, or competitor claims.

### Concept 1 — Desk to trail, without changing bags
- **Creative type:** Lifestyle demonstration / routine transition
- **Angle:** For commuters who go from weekday work to a short weekend outing and want one practical bag for both routines.
- **Headline:** **One daypack. Workday to weekend.**
- **Body:** The Daypack 18L carries your commute essentials with an external bottle pocket and padded 13-inch laptop sleeve—then comes along for short trips. Water-resistant fabric helps with light weather; it is not waterproof.
- **CTA:** **Shop Now**
- **Image composition:** Split-scene or diagonal transition. Left side: restrained desk setup with the Daypack beside a laptop. Right side: simple weekend trailhead or travel setting with the same bag. Make the bag the largest product element and keep the background uncluttered. Put the headline in the upper third, one short supporting line beneath it, and the CTA/product identification in the lower third.
- **Production instructions:** Use one consistent bag image across both environments so the transition is immediately clear. Avoid staged adventure cues, dramatic landscapes, or copy implying technical outdoor performance. Ensure the laptop sleeve and bottle pocket are visible or clearly represented. Keep text large enough for mobile; do not place copy over the product.

### Concept 2 — Resolve the 15-inch laptop question
- **Creative type:** Objection-handling / specification callout
- **Angle:** For shoppers considering the Daypack but uncertain about laptop compatibility. Answer the question transparently rather than implying a 15-inch fit.
- **Headline:** **Have a 15-inch laptop? Check before you order.**
- **Body:** The Daypack 18L has a padded sleeve sized for a 13-inch laptop. If you carry a 15-inch device, confirm its dimensions against the product details before purchasing.
- **CTA:** **Shop Now**
- **Image composition:** Clean product-on-background layout with a visible 13-inch laptop partially inserted into the sleeve. Add a simple, non-technical label: **“Padded 13-inch laptop sleeve.”** Place the 15-inch question as the dominant headline, followed immediately by the honest answer. Keep the bag and laptop large enough to understand at feed speed.
- **Production instructions:** Do not illustrate or imply a 15-inch laptop inside the bag. Do not use a measurement graphic unless Shopify provides verified bag and sleeve dimensions. Link to the Daypack product page, where the laptop information should appear above reviews if possible.

### Concept 3 — The practical bag for two routines
- **Creative type:** USP callout / one-element positioning hypothesis
- **Angle:** Test whether “practical and restrained” outperforms adventure-led positioning for commuters taking short weekend trips.
- **Headline:** **Pack for the day. Keep it useful on the weekend.**
- **Body:** Daypack 18L: padded 13-inch laptop sleeve, external bottle pocket, and water-resistant fabric. Free US shipping; estimated delivery is 4–7 business days.
- **CTA:** **Shop Now**
- **Image composition:** Minimal still-life: Daypack centered on a plain, warm-neutral background with only three nearby essentials—a laptop, bottle, and compact weekend layer. Use the headline as the main attention magnet, then three short feature callouts around the product. Keep the logo small and secondary.
- **Production instructions:** Use restrained typography, generous spacing, and no badges such as “best,” “waterproof,” or “built to last.” The first two seconds of viewing should communicate the product, audience, and practical use case without requiring a caption read.

### Single-variable test plan
Build all three as **4:5 static ads** with the same Daypack PDP, **Shop Now** CTA, no discount, identical audience settings, placements, attribution settings, and campaign budget. The intended variable is the **message angle**: transition use case vs. laptop objection vs. practical two-routine positioning. Do not make simultaneous changes to image format, offer, landing page, or audience.

Use equal initial delivery where the platform permits. Review spend, outbound CTR, landing-page views, add-to-cart rate, checkout starts, and purchases. Do not use CTR alone to declare a winner. Because Shopify orders have declined while traffic increased and inventory is constrained, keep the test controlled and avoid aggressive scaling until stock and replenishment timing are reviewed.

**Designer allocation: 8 hours total:** Concept 1: 3 hours; Concept 2: 2.5 hours; Concept 3: 2.5 hours. Export editable source files plus 4:5, 1:1, and 9:16 crops only if the composition remains legible; the primary test asset is 4:5.

input.reference_guidance:
[377393f355c6053df5e1edc3] Write creative briefs with six mandatory fields before producing ads
Applies when: Handing off a static ad to a designer or producing it yourself in Canva.
- After research, write a brief per ad. Include these fields: (1) Concept, (2) Creative type — curiosity static, us-versus-them, USP callout, social-proof/review, etc. (3) Angle — what you are actually doing and who you are selling to. (4) Headline. (5) CTA. (6) Visual direction.
- Always name the creative type explicitly so your set stays diverse and you do not make one hundred near-identical variants.
- Use the brief as the production spec: ship it to a designer's attention or review your own brief and build the ad in Canva.
- Treat each field as a decision to make deliberately — a missing creative-type or angle field is the fastest route to a monotone, undifferentiated set of ads.
Condition: This is the presenter's own briefing framework; adapt the field list to your team's handoff format.

[08f49b8491b0ead3b3cc138b] Design Static Ads Around the Eye's Reading Path
Applies when: Laying out a static ad image and deciding what element goes where to maximise cold-audience attention and comprehension.
- Place the single strongest attention magnet first — usually a headline in large type or a striking background image that stands out against the feed. The source's best-in-class example (a protein coffee drink static) led with a bold centre headline plus an unusual background image.
- Use the image to open a question the headline then answers (or vice versa): the reader should think 'what is this drink?' and the headline '2-in-1 mocktail and protein fix' should resolve it. This image-headline tension is what generates the click.
- Close the curiosity gap immediately with one bold, concise line of explanation in the centre — don't make the reader hunt through the ad to learn what the product is.
- Add short supporting bullets only for information needed to understand the product; the reference ad used 'grass-fed Aussie whey, 100% real coffee and chocolate'.
- Finish with social proof and a clear product visual so the buyer is confident the product will look like what's advertised — the source compares this to avoiding a 'McDonald's photo shoot' gap between ad and reality.
- Audit the failure mode: awkward spacing, an oversized logo, confusing graphs or sub-headlines too small to read on an iPhone break this flow and destroy authority. Enlarge unreadable supporting text by roughly 30% in the source's estimate and shift the product to free layout room.
Condition: This is design craft guidance drawn from deconstructing eight statics, not a measured benchmark; the 30% enlargement is a presenter's suggested fix, not tested data.
Condition: The source's claim that the reference static would 'flop' without its background image is an opinion about that specific ad, not a general law.

[1c4808b43997d5b85feb4b1c] Run single-variable creative tests within the same angle
Applies when: You have a promising angle and want to learn something rather than randomly produce new ads.
- Take one validated angle — e.g. 'get your steps in while you work without needing a giant treadmill' — and produce two versions that share the same product and argument.
- Example pairing from the source: version one as a UGC video, version two as a carousel where the slides tell the story, with a different opening format but the same underlying angle.
- Run them in an apples-to-apples environment where each gets equal visibility, then read the data to identify why one was better.
- Never change the hook, angle, audience, landing page, offer, campaign and creative simultaneously — the source's point is that if performance changes you will have no idea which change caused it.
- After isolating the winner, cut the weaker version and carry the learning into the next brief, focusing on how to make a better version of what worked (the source suggests more before-and-after and routine footage as a next step in its example).
Condition: The source acknowledges that video versus carousel is a large format difference; the principle is to control as much as possible, not that all format comparisons are perfectly clean.
Condition: Format is only a variable to test once the angle itself is defined — the source explicitly de-prioritizes starting from format.

[ab5dac71c1dc0cd369d1d52c] Concept = Persona × Angle × Offer × Format
Applies when: Planning a static ad test batch for your store and deciding which changes count as new concepts versus minor design tweaks.
- Define four slots for every concept: who it's for (persona), the persuasive angle, the offer, and the format (native, advertorial, before/after, listicle, feature call-out).
- Only count a new ad as a new concept when at least one of those four elements genuinely changes.
- Discard or deprioritize tests that only change a background color, font, or minor layout — the source argues these are grouped by Meta's algorithm (Andromeda) under the same Entity ID, so no real learning is produced.
- Keep a concept grid so your team can see coverage gaps — e.g., many angles for one persona but no offers for another.
- Prioritize concept breadth over polish depth when planning the week's output.
Condition: The Andromeda Entity ID grouping is the source's explanation of Meta's current behavior; verify against the current Meta interface and documentation as it evolves.
Condition: Some minor visual refinement still matters for a finished ad — the point is not to count it as a separate test.

[4a3ce680ae23e5eb6e943fd6] Testing Priority Order: Angle First, Then Offer, Persona, Format
Applies when: Diagnosing why ads are underperforming and deciding what variable to test next.
- Rank the four levers in the source's order: (1) angle, (2) offer, (3) persona, (4) format. The source says most teams invert this and spend all their time testing formats.
- Angle first: if you are targeting personas who already purchase from you, and they still aren't buying, the problem is message or argument. Rotate and improve the angle.
- Offer second: it may be the single most important variable, but flexibility is limited. With one or two products you cannot change the product, and offer variants (bundles, gift with purchase, tiered discounts, subscriptions) eventually run out. The source warns against solving this with heavy discounts that eat margin and create discount dependence.
- Persona third: it is mainly what gives you breadth and volume once angle and offer are dialled in.
- Format last: 'UGC doesn't work' is the wrong lesson — the script, persona, angle and offer inside the format are what work. Same for professional photo shoots.
Condition: The source treats the ranking as a practical heuristic, not an absolute law, and notes offer is arguably the most important variable in theory.
Condition: The claim that most accounts do not need broad-audience unaware ads is the presenter's opinion based on their client experience.

[7272fafc80c75a09a6cd3508] The One-Element Ad — Strip To The Essential Component
Applies when: You are designing static ads or PDP hero blocks with too much going on and want to increase stopping power.
- Start from the default spec — header, subheader, picture, logo — and then ask whether you can do the ad with just one of those.
- Source cites Neil French via the episode: if you can do an ad with just one of those elements, you're onto a winner.
- Worked example: the Economist 'I've never read The Economist — management trainee, aged 42' ad has no apparent subheader, no picture, and the logo absent in the standard position; the ad's identity comes from brand colour and the word 'Economist' embedded in the copy.
- For ecommerce translation: test a static ad or PDP hero that is one compelling sentence and one visual, or even just one sentence, rather than the standard headline + subhead + CTA stack.
- Keep the identification cues the brand owns (colour, distinctive typography, a recognisable phrase) so the stripped ad is still attributed to you, as the source notes for the Economist red.
- Sequence is deliberate: the source points to the first line causing a question and the second line resolving it — 'It takes 3.1 seconds to read this ad / the same time it takes a Model S to go 0-60'.
- Apply the One Mississippi, Two Mississippi check to the reduced ad before shipping.
Condition: The source's claim that one-element ads are 'a winner' is Neil French's craft opinion relayed by the presenter, not a measured rule.
Condition: Reduction can cost clarity for shoppers who scan for price, specification or shipping information; the stripped creative may need a denser supporting block on the same page.

[9197d49f4af43881e5fb28e4] Common hook types and when to use each
Applies when: Choosing an angle for a new ecommerce ad, or generating a set of hook variations to test against a control.
- Contrarian truth: 'The advice everyone follows is backwards because…' followed by an educational payoff. Works well in paid and organic.
- Specific proof: 'We did X and got Y in Z days. Here's what actually caused it.' Cited as a strong performer.
- Common mistakes: 'The number one mistake brands make when scaling.' The source uses it but warns it is heavily overused and has lost weight with audiences.
- High-stakes warning: 'If you're using protein powder, you're slowly destroying your gut.' The source uses this frequently in ecommerce and notes it lets you swap the warning to resonate with different audience pools.
- Curiosity gap: create an information gap in the hook and even in the thumbnail/copy. For statics, infomercial-style images that explain nothing (e.g., a symptom with no explanation) can produce very high CTR.
- Tactical promise: 'In 90 seconds I'll give you the exact checklist…' — the source notes this suits service businesses more than ecom.
- Mythbusting objection: 'If you think X, you're not wrong. Here's how to tell if yours is the exception.' Adapts to ecommerce by busting myths about your product category.
Condition: Most common does not mean best — if competitors saturate a hook type, look for white space, though doubling down on what competitors do can also work.
Condition: Curiosity-gap statics can attract junk clickthroughs from people not primed to buy; the source says they require dropping traffic onto a long educational/listical landing page that sells only at the end.
Condition: Numeric claims in example hooks (days, percentages) are illustrative, not validated benchmarks.
